title: Running it: roles, configuration, deployment, and what is not built
summary: farmd is one static binary with thirteen subcommands; every role is a subcommand so a reaper can never run a different commit than the scheduler it races with. This page is the authoritative configuration reference — 28 variables in internal/config plus 7 read elsewhere, four of which are validated at boot and then ignored — and the honest inventory of what is not wired. Four entries that used to head that inventory are closed: authentication is chosen by configuration, `farmd node` starts, the recovery ladder has a client for the host agent, and a Helm chart ships. What remains is the metrics gap, and it is worse than it used to read: /metrics carries no package's own series at all, because cmd/farmd/roles.go calls obs.RegisterAll with no collector groups and the tree's single Collectors() call site sits in a branch farmd never takes. The one thing to carry away: SIGTERM drains work and releases nothing, deliberately.

sections.heading: The twelve subcommands, and which one you are starting
sections.body:
`farmd` with no arguments prints usage to **stderr** and exits **2**. `farmd --help` prints byte-identical text to **stdout** and exits **0**. Both answer without touching the environment or the database, so they still work in a scratch container and in a broken deployment: the `help`/`version` switch in cmd/farmd/main.go runs before `context.WithCancel` and before any call to config.Load.

There is no default role. The Dockerfile sets `ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/farmd"]` with no CMD, so a manifest with a typo fails instead of starting something plausible.

Exit codes are distinct on purpose: 0 success, 1 failure, 2 you typed it wrong, 3 role not implemented. **Exit 3 is currently unreachable** — `notImplemented` is defined at cmd/farmd/main.go:236 and has no callers.

One quirk to know before you debug a manifest: `runRole` defines the demo's `-hosts` and `-devices` flags on the flag set for *every* role, so `farmd scheduler -hosts 9` parses and is ignored. A typo'd flag is a usage error whose help text then lists `-devices` and `-hosts` — both labelled "demo only:", which is the only thing that saves it from being actively misleading.
bullets: `api`, `scheduler`, `reaper`, `watchdog`, `recovery`, `jobrunner`, `node`, `all`, `demo` all go through `runRole`: config preflight, then pool dial + ping, then dispatch. A bad manifest fails at rollout, not at the first request.
`ctl` loads config with `WithoutDatabase()` and never opens Postgres — it must keep working when the control plane is the thing being investigated.
`migrate` also loads with `WithoutDatabase()` (cmd/farmd/migrate.go:150) because `-dsn` is allowed to be the only source of a DSN.
`all` runs api + scheduler + reaper + recovery + jobrunner + one watchdog per registered host in one process. It does **not** include `node`.
`demo` is `all` plus `internal/demo`, which owns the fake hardware. The scheduler, lease store, reaper, recovery ladder and job runner are the production code paths.

sections.heading: Why some roles elect a leader and some just race
sections.body:
Two mechanisms, chosen for two different reasons.

**Advisory-lock leader election (scheduler, reaper).** Both loops make *global* decisions — which of the farm's free devices goes to which queued job; which suspect leases become reclaimable. Two of them running is not slower, it is wrong. Each holds a Postgres **session** advisory lock on a connection checked out of the pool and kept for as long as leadership lasts (scheduler.go:631-668, reaper.go:551).

Three details are load-bearing:

- The lock is never taken with the blocking `pg_advisory_lock`. A standby that blocked would hold a pool connection open forever waiting for a leader that may never yield.
- The leadership check doubles as a `Ping` on that connection, and losing the connection is treated as losing leadership *immediately*. A checked-out connection whose backend died still looks fine to the pool, and it is exempt from the pool's idle and lifetime reaping — which is exactly the property being relied on.
- On a clean shutdown the lock is explicitly unlocked, so a rolling deploy hands leadership over in milliseconds rather than waiting out a TCP timeout.

The reaper adds one rule: on every **gain** of leadership it calls `farm.reaper_arm` *before* its first sweep (reaper.go:243-258). Until arm returns, every live lease still carries the deadline it had before the outage and the quiesce gate is unset. If arm fails the reaper releases leadership and stands down rather than sweeping unarmed — a reaper that sweeps without a refund charges tenants for the control plane's downtime, and the leases most at risk are the ones that were silent the longest.

**SKIP LOCKED claiming (jobrunner).** A job runner makes a *local* decision — take this job, run it here. N replicas taking different jobs is the point. Correctness comes from three independent guards described in the package doc at internal/jobrunner/jobrunner.go, and behind all three sits the database: if two replicas ever did attach to one job, the second `Acquire` takes over renewal and the first is fenced at its next renewal, which becomes an abandoned attempt without another byte written to the device.
bullets: Job advisory keys carry the prefix "device-farmer/jobrunner:" before the FNV hash because the one-argument bigint advisory space is shared with the scheduler's and the reaper's leadership keys (`claimKey`, jobrunner.go).

On shutdown the jobrunner names its keys instead of calling `pg_advisory_unlock_all()` — that would clear the leadership locks too and hand leadership away as a side effect of a jobrunner stopping (`claimLocks.close`, jobrunner.go:1451-1462).

`farm.lease_mark_suspect`, `farm.lease_reclaim` and `farm.lease_expire_max_runtime` are all LIMIT-bounded and use `FOR NO KEY UPDATE … SKIP LOCKED` (00002_lease.sql:490, :559, :603), so a bounded batch that loses a race picks the row up next cycle.

examples.label: Who holds the leadership locks right now
examples.code:
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -P footer=off -c "
SELECT pid,
       CASE classid::bigint * 4294967296 + objid::bigint
         WHEN x'6661726d5363686c'::bigint THEN 'scheduler leader'
         WHEN x'6661726d52656170'::bigint THEN 'reaper leader'
         ELSE 'jobrunner claim (per job)' END AS what
  FROM pg_locks WHERE locktype = 'advisory' ORDER BY 2;"
examples.output:
pid  |       what       
-------+------------------
 14000 | reaper leader
 27152 | scheduler leader
examples.note: Run against the live demo. `pid` is the Postgres backend, not the farmd process — one farmd process shows two rows because each loop owns its own checked-out connection. In production the useful reading is the row count against the replica count: exactly one of each, always. Sampled three times a few seconds apart and saw no jobrunner claim row; those exist only while a job is actually running and the demo's jobs are short.

sections.heading: Configuration reference: the 28 variables internal/config reads
sections.body:
There is nowhere else to get this. `internal/config/config.go` is the only place these names exist, and the package's rule is that every violation is reported at once so you fix a manifest in one edit rather than five deploys.

An empty or whitespace-only value is treated as **unset** (`loader.raw` trims and returns `"", false`). You cannot blank a variable to disable it; you get the default. That single behaviour is what makes `farmd node` unstartable — see the gaps.

Durations use Go syntax: `90s`, `15m`, `2h`. A malformed duration is collected as a parse error and reported alongside every other parse error before any semantic validation runs, because validating a value you failed to parse produces noise that buries the real problem.

Note what none of these knobs can do: none of them shortens or ends a lease in response to a transport event. The only clocks here that can end a lease are `FARM_LEASE_TTL` + `FARM_LEASE_GRACE`, and they measure the *renewal* wire to Postgres, never the ADB wire to the phone.
bullets: `DATABASE_URL` accepts both the libpq URL form (`postgres://…`) and the keyword/value form (`host=db user=farm sslmode=require`). Anything else is rejected at boot rather than inside a CrashLoopBackOff.

Passwords are redacted in every log line and error: `RedactedDatabaseURL()` blanks userinfo passwords *and* the `password`/`sslpassword` query parameters, because `url.Redacted()` alone misses the query form.
`FARM_COMPONENT` is honoured by the **api role only**. Every other role hardcodes its component name in cmd/farmd/roles.go. Read the gap on this before you rely on it.

`farm.reaper_arm` treats `now() - min(beat_at)` above this as a control-plane outage and refunds it to every live lease. Must be positive.

The components whose **oldest existing** beat defines the gap. A named component with no row at all is skipped, not treated as stale. A component on the renewal path that is missing here is a blind spot big enough to mass-reclaim the farm (BLOCKER 8, migrations/00002_lease.sql:417).

The ADB server this host's node agent and single-host watchdog talk to.
Which physical host this process speaks for. **Required** by `node`. Selects single-host mode for `watchdog`.
Overrides the embedded SQL. Setting it suppresses the "migrations discovered on disk" warning, because an operator who set it already knows.

sections.heading: Seven more variables, and four knobs that do nothing
sections.body:
Not everything farmd reads lives in `internal/config`. These seven are read directly by the package that owns the concern — authentication is `internal/api`'s business, and `config.Config` is shared by every role in the binary, most of which serve no HTTP at all.

Four documented knobs are validated at startup and then reach nothing, or reach exactly one role. This matters more than it sounds: `config.Summary()` prints `renew / witness = 1m30s / 2m0s`, `/api/v1/capabilities` reports `"renew_interval": "1m30s"`, and neither number reaches any code. An operator who lowers the renew interval to survive a slow Postgres gets a boot-time cross-check against the TTL, two reassuring readouts, and no behavioural change whatsoever. FARM_API_TOKENS and FARM_API_AUTH used to be on this list and are not any more — they are wired, and the table above says what they now do.
bullets: **FARM_LEASE_RENEW_INTERVAL** — validated (≥3 renewal attempts must fit inside the TTL) but `cmd/farmd/roles.go:runJobRunner` never sets `jobrunner.Config.HolderConfig` (the field exists at jobrunner.go:194), so `lease.Holder` falls back to `DefaultRenewInterval = 60s` (holder.go:24). The same 60s also fixes the takeover window, since `DefaultTakeover = 3 * lease.DefaultRenewInterval` (jobrunner.go:140). The 90s you configured is not the 60s that runs.

**FARM_LEASE_WITNESS_INTERVAL / FARM_LEASE_WITNESS_MAX_EXTENSIONS** — `farm.lease_witness` exists in SQL (00002_lease.sql:355), `lease.Store.Witness` (store.go:284), `Holder.Witness` (holder.go:316), `Holder.StartWitness` and the `WitnessLoop` (witness.go:216) all exist and are tested, and the on-device marker that produces the evidence exists in internal/runner/witness.go. **Nothing on a placement path constructs either.** No witness loop is started by internal/jobrunner or internal/runner, and no `/witness` route exists, so these two values still change nothing.

**FARM_METRICS_ADDR** — appears in config.go and in the Summary string and is never passed to `net.Listen`. /metrics is served on FARM_API_ADDR. The Dockerfile's `EXPOSE 9090` documents a port nothing binds.

**FARM_SHUTDOWN_GRACE** — validated for every role and consumed by exactly one file, `internal/api/server.go:459`, where it bounds in-flight request draining. On a scheduler, reaper, jobrunner, janitor, recovery or watchdog it is checked at boot and then ignored, so the value you set describes only the roles that serve HTTP.

A comma-separated list of `<token>:<role>[:<subject>[:<tenant>]]`. The deliberate opt-in to serving with no authentication at all. It exists because an evaluation farm and a manifest whose FARM_API_TOKENS line was lost in a merge look identical from inside the process; nobody writes this by accident.

sections.heading: The startup assertions that refuse a manifest
sections.body:
Configuration is validated *before* the role starts and before the database is dialled. Every violation is reported together. Two assertions are worth knowing by heart because they are the ones that cost devices.

**The slot-rearm assertion.** `FARM_SLOT_REARM` must exceed `FARM_NODE_SELF_FENCE_TIMEOUT` by at least `FARM_FENCE_SAFETY_MARGIN`. When a lease is reclaimed the device gets a new fence floor and the slot is parked for the rearm interval. The node proxy only discovers its fence is stale after its self-fence timeout elapses; until then it is still holding ADB sockets open and still forwarding the old job's commands. If the slot becomes schedulable before that teardown finishes, two tenants share one phone — shell commands interleave, installs land in the wrong session, and neither side sees an error. Nothing downstream can detect it, which is why it is refused here.

**The BLOCKER 8 assertion.** If the role or the component name is on the renewal path (`api`, `scheduler`, `reaper`) it must appear in `FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS`. The check consults the *role* as well as the name specifically so that `FARM_COMPONENT=api-canary` cannot switch the guard off for a process that is still very much on the renewal path. Read the gaps: the same assertion has two holes it does not cover.

The rest, in one list: TTL ≥ 10m and grace ≥ 5m (mirroring the schema CHECKs, so an acquire never dies with SQLSTATE 23514 while a tenant waits); at least 3 renewal attempts inside one TTL; witness interval ≤ half the grace band; heartbeat interval ≤ half the gap floor; gap floor, reaper interval, shutdown grace, watchdog interval, self-fence timeout and DB connect timeout all positive; fence margin not negative; batch ≥ 1; max conns ≥ 1; at least one reaper component; component name matching `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]*` and ≤ 63 chars; FARM_API_URL absolute with an http/https scheme.

sections.heading: Three ways to bring it up
sections.body:
All three end at the same place: Postgres, schema at version 4, and a control plane on `http://127.0.0.1:8420`.

**1. `scripts/dev-up.ps1` — Windows, no Docker.** Creates a *throwaway* PostgreSQL cluster under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\device-farmer\pgdata` on port 55432, listening only on 127.0.0.1 with trust auth. It never touches an existing PostgreSQL service. If something is already listening on the port it reuses it rather than fighting over it. `-Reset` stops the cluster with `pg_ctl -m immediate`, deletes the data directory, re-runs initdb and then continues into the normal bring-up; `-NoDemo` stops after the migration so you can start a role yourself. This is what is running behind the live system this page was written against.

**2. `make demo` — Linux/macOS, or Git Bash with GNU make.** `build` → `migrate` → `demo -hosts 2 -devices 56`, against `DATABASE_URL` (default: the same 55432 cluster), with FARM_API_ADDR defaulted to 127.0.0.1:8420. GNU make is *not* present on a stock Windows box — that is why dev-up.ps1 exists. `make test` also enforces `gofmt -l` being empty, which will fail a tree with unformatted files even if it compiles.

**3. `docker compose up -d` — everything in containers.** Postgres 17-alpine with a `pg_isready` healthcheck, a one-shot `migrate` service every other service waits on with `condition: service_completed_successfully`, then `demo`. A failed migration stops the rollout instead of starting a control plane against a schema it does not understand. Postgres is published on `127.0.0.1:55433` for psql and for `test/assertions.sql`; the comment beside it says to drop that line for anything that is not a laptop.

**Do not use `docker compose --profile farm up -d` as written.** The `demo` service carries no `profiles:` key, so Compose starts it alongside the six farm services — simulated hardware writing into the same database as your real control plane — and both `demo` and `api` publish `${FARM_PORT:-8420}`, so the second one to start fails to bind. The file's own header says to "drop the `demo` service", but the `--profile farm` instruction fifty lines lower does not repeat it.
bullets: The `farm` profile has no `node` service, correctly: `farmd node` needs `/dev/bus/usb` on the physical machine and cannot live in the cluster.
`make assertions` runs `test/assertions.sql` — the lease protocol as executable specification — against a live Postgres. It needs `psql` on PATH.
The Dockerfile runs `go vet ./... && go test ./...` in the build stage *after* producing the binary, so a failing test fails the image but does not save you the build.

  Watch for the line "device dropped offline mid-lease". The lease must NOT

sections.heading: The schema, and farmd migrate
sections.body:
The migrations are **embedded in the binary**. `//go:embed` patterns may not contain `..` or leave the package directory, so `cmd/farmd` cannot embed `../../migrations` itself; `migrations/embed.go` embeds its own `*.sql` and `cmd/farmd/embed.go` adopts them into the `migrationsFS` variable. The effect is that an image which shipped the binary without the SQL would otherwise migrate to version 0, report success, and leave a running control plane pointed at an empty database. The `migrations` package also panics at init if the embedded set is empty, has a duplicate version number, or is missing `00001_core.sql` — a missing image layer must look like a broken build, not a clean deploy.

If the embed is ever lost, `resolveMigrations` falls back to searching the working directory, its parents and the directory holding the binary — and warns loudly, but only when the directory was *guessed*. If you passed `-dir` or set `FARM_MIGRATIONS_DIR` you already know, and a warning you cannot act on trains you to ignore the ones you can.

A session-scoped advisory lock on one dedicated `*sql.Conn` serialises concurrent migrators (a pooled handle would unlock on a connection you no longer own), so it is safe to run `farmd migrate up` as a Job with more than one replica or a retrying init container. `status` deliberately does **not** take the lock — that is exactly when you want to look.

`down-to` refuses to move backwards without `-yes`, because the down migrations drop `farm.leases`: the record of which jobs own which devices. The phones keep running; nothing in the control plane would know.

sections.heading: Deploying a real farm, and the hardware underneath it
sections.body:
The USB tier cannot move into the cluster. That is physics, not a design limitation. Everything else can.

**In the cluster:** `api` (scale freely), `scheduler` (N replicas, one leader), `jobrunner` (scale freely), `reaper` (N replicas, one leader), `watchdog` (one per host, named by FARM_HOST_ID), `recovery`. Plus Postgres, which holds all state.

**On each USB host, outside the cluster:** an ADB server in a privileged container, and `farmd node` (which cannot start in this build — see the gaps).

```
docker run -d --name adbd --privileged --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 5037:5037 -v /dev/bus/usb:/dev/bus/usb devicefarmer/adb:latest/n```

The cluster's watchdog and recovery ladder reach each host's ADB server over TCP on 5037, so `farm.hosts.adb_endpoint` must be an address the cluster network can route to.

**The hardware shape.** 28 devices per host — four powered 7-port hubs on a dedicated PCIe USB 3.0 card — is STF's own reference build (README.md), and it is the shape `internal/demo/seed.go` seeds (`DefaultHubsPerHost = 4`, `DefaultSlotsPerHub = 7`). Plan two hosts for 50–60 handsets, three if you want to drain one for maintenance without stopping.

**Ganged vs switchable decides whether recovery tier 4 exists for a device.** `internal/topo/sysfs.go` requires *positive evidence* of per-port switching: `Switchable()` returns true only for `PerPortPower`, and `UnknownPower` — the kernel exposed nothing readable — is reported as not switchable. Absence of evidence is never read as capability, because a hub wrongly marked per-port would let the ladder cut power to seven devices, six of them mid-run holding live leases, while believing it had touched one. Discovery then calls `farm.register_slot`, which maps not-switchable to a single **ganged** domain with `control='none'` for the whole hub (migrations/00004_operate.sql:419).

One caveat when reading the demo's topology below: the demo does **not** go through `register_slot`. `internal/demo/seed.go` inserts into `farm.power_domains` directly and its `planPower` assigns a fourth kind, `'none'`, that real discovery never produces. Treat the `none` rows as a seeded case for exercising the refusal path, not as something you will see on a discovered host.

And tier 4 needs **Linux 6.0 or newer**. Below that the USB core re-powers a port that was switched off behind its back (internal/node/uhubctl.go:31-41): uhubctl reports success, the port never went dark, and the ladder would learn that tier 4 "was tried and did not help", then escalate to quarantining a device whose only real problem is that the one rung that would have fixed it was never performed. `checkKernelFloor` (uhubctl.go:210-226) refuses the whole rung on such a kernel instead, with a message naming the fix.
bullets: `farmd watchdog` with FARM_HOST_ID set supervises one host — the production shape, one pod per host. Without it, it supervises every non-disabled row in `farm.hosts` in one process, and errors out if there are none.
Draining a host stops new placement and releases nothing. `ctl hosts` prints LIVE LEASES precisely because that is what a drain has to wait out.

The node agent's heartbeat must **not** be in FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS: `farm.reaper_arm` adds each named component's downtime to every live lease's deadline, and letting a host agent's outage move lease clocks would fuse the hardware plane into lease liveness. internal/node/agent.go:1174 says so in the metric help text.

sections.heading: Shutdown: SIGTERM drains work and releases nothing
sections.body:
This is the section to read before a rolling deploy.

SIGTERM and SIGINT cancel the root context. Cancellation means *stop accepting new work and finish what is in flight*. It does **not** mean *release the leases this process holds*, and no code reachable from `cmd/farmd/main.go` may make it mean that.

The reason is the whole thesis. In Kubernetes a SIGTERM is the most ordinary event there is: a node drain, a rolling update, a spot preemption, an OOM restart, an HPA scale-down. None of those is evidence that the job on the phone died. A pod that "cleans up after itself" by releasing its leases converts routine cluster churn into destroyed work — DeviceFarmer/STF issue #663 with a Kubernetes trigger instead of a socket one.

So the replacement pod calls `farm.lease_acquire` with the same `job_id` and Phase 1 (migrations/00002_lease.sql:206-229) returns the same lease, the same device and the **same fence**, with `reattached = true`. It bumps `holder`, `holder_instance`, `holder_epoch` and the heartbeat, and extends the deadlines with `GREATEST(existing, now() + ttl)` so a re-attach can never shorten a lease. The fence is deliberately not bumped, because the job's own work may still be running detached on the device and bumping would fence out its own process. The runner then resumes from `farm.jobs.checkpoint`.

If the replacement never arrives, the lease ends the way every lease without a holder ends: heartbeats stop, the suspect sweep marks it (marking releases nothing, and a heartbeat anywhere in the grace band heals it back to `held` at the same fence with zero work lost), the grace band elapses, and `farm.lease_reclaim` takes it back. That path has a control-plane gap refund and a quiesce gate in front of it. A local `os.Exit` has neither, which is exactly why it does not get to make the decision.

**A second signal restores the default disposition.** An impatient operator pressing Ctrl-C twice gets an immediate kill.
bullets: The signal handler is a plain channel rather than `signal.NotifyContext`, so the shutdown banner fires on an actual signal and not merely on the root context ending — otherwise every ordinary exit would claim to have been evicted.

The API's `http.Server.BaseContext` is deliberately **not** the run context (server.go:407-412). If it were, cancelling would kill every in-flight request at the same instant, including a renewal one round trip from succeeding.

Event streams are closed *first* in `Shutdown` (server.go:482-486), otherwise `http.Shutdown` would burn the entire grace period on connections that are healthy and idle by design, and real in-flight requests would be cut off when it expired.
There is no `WriteTimeout` on the API server: `GET /api/v1/stream` is long-lived. Slow-loris protection is `ReadHeaderTimeout: 10s` plus `IdleTimeout: 120s`.
If the grace period expires with background bulk work still running, the server logs "shutdown grace expired with background work still running; no lease was released" and returns anyway.
`pool.Close()` in `runRole` ends this process's connections. It ends no lease.

In the jobrunner, an outcome with an **empty** ReleaseReason — an abandoned attempt, a SIGTERM mid-run — must leave the lease alive: it is what the replacement re-attaches to. Every release site asks `lease.Holder.Fenced` first, because a re-attach hands the replacement the *same* fence, so a fenced process still presents a fence that matches and the database alone cannot tell the two apart.

A socket error, a probe timeout or a device going offline has no word to write here, so "released because the transport dropped" raises check_violation rather than silently destroying six hours of work. Over 1096 leases on this farm, every ending is one a job, a deadline or a human caused.

sections.heading: What you can see while it runs
sections.body:
Four unauthenticated infrastructure routes, one authenticated everything-else. A liveness probe that needs a credential is a liveness probe that fails when the credential rotates, and an operator debugging a farm whose auth is the broken thing still needs to see its state.

`/api/v1/capabilities` (internal/api/capabilities.go) is the one to open first at 3am: it reports build, schema version, the authentication posture in plain words, which components are heartbeating, and which features are consequently unavailable — observed rather than declared. On the live demo it correctly reports `node: running false`, `enroll: running false`, `Dynamic enrollment: unavailable` and `Authentication: not_built`.

`/metrics` is where the honesty runs out. `cmd/farmd/roles.go:newRegistry` builds a bare `prometheus.NewRegistry()` and calls **only** `obs.Register`. Nine packages define a `Collectors()` function — adbwire, enroll, jobrunner, node, reaper, recovery, scheduler, topo, watchdog — and not one is ever registered. Neither are the Go runtime or process collectors. Seventeen metric families are exposed; `farm_scheduler_leader` and `farm_reaper_leader`, the two gauges whose sum across replicas must equal 1, are not among them.
bullets: `/healthz` — liveness. Component name and uptime. No database call.
`/readyz` — readiness, bounded by a 2s database probe. Short on purpose: a probe that hangs is a probe that fails open.
`/metrics` — Prometheus, on the API's own listener (FARM_METRICS_ADDR binds nothing).
`/api/v1/capabilities` — build, schema, auth posture, per-component liveness and per-feature availability.
Everything under `/api/v1/` else goes through `requireRole`, which today grants every caller the operator role.

sections.heading: Roadmap, in the order the code argues for
sections.body: Ordered by what unblocks what, not by what reads well in a release note. Items 1–2 are the difference between a control plane and a device farm; 3–6 are cheap fixes to things that are actively wrong at defaults; 7–11 follow.
bullets: **1. Make `farmd node` startable.** Add a `FARM_NODE_TOKEN` to internal/config and pass it through `runNode`; default `node.Config.Component` to `"node:" + hostID` as the package already intends (agent.go:114-117, 250-251) instead of the hardcoded `"node"`. Every claim in this repo about real hardware — and all of dynamic enrollment — is downstream of a node agent that can construct itself.

**2. Give the recovery role a HostRunner.** Write the HTTP client for `POST /node/v1/usb-reset` and `/node/v1/port-power`, resolve each host's node endpoint from `farm.hosts`, and pass it to `recovery.NewADBActuator` instead of `nil`. Until this ships, tiers 3 and 4 of a nine-rung ladder can never execute anywhere. Second because it is meaningless without 1.

**3. Turn authentication on.** Replace `api.WithAuthenticator(api.NewAllowAll(log, "anonymous"))` at roles.go:148 with `api.AuthenticatorFromEnv(log)` — already written, already tested, and it refuses to fall back to open unless `FARM_API_AUTH=allow-all` says so deliberately. One line plus the compose/manifest change. Before the Helm chart, because a chart that ships open auth is worse than no chart.

**4. Honour FARM_COMPONENT in every role, or stop validating it in every role.** Right now the BLOCKER 8 assertion checks a name that only the `api` role will ever write. Pass `cfg.Component` through in roles.go (keeping the `watchdog:<host>` suffix), or make the preflight say plainly that the knob is api-only.

**5. Fix the gap-accounting defaults.** Add `jobrunner` to `DefaultReaperComponents`, and extend `onRenewalPath` to cover `jobrunner`, `all` and `demo`. This is a data-loss bug at defaults: the exact BLOCKER 8 shape the config package exists to prevent, reached through a component the assertion does not cover.

**6. Register the collectors.** Nine `Collectors()` calls in `newRegistry`, plus `collectors.NewGoCollector()` and `NewProcessCollector()`. You cannot today alert on "exactly one scheduler leader", on reaper arm failures, on jobrunner beat failures, or on watchdog host coverage — and items 4 and 5 are hard to verify without them.

**7. Wire or delete the four dead knobs.** Pass `FARM_LEASE_RENEW_INTERVAL` into `jobrunner.Config.HolderConfig`; either build the witness loop the SQL and the Holder are already waiting for, or remove both witness variables, their cross-checks and the `renew / witness` summary line; either bind `FARM_METRICS_ADDR` or delete it and the Dockerfile's `EXPOSE 9090`. A configuration summary that lies is worse than a missing knob.
**8. Give the compose `demo` service its own profile.** One line. It stops `--profile farm up` from starting simulated hardware against a real database and colliding on port 8420.

**9. Helm chart in `deploy/helm` (currently an empty directory).** After 3 and 6, so the chart encodes the auth and metrics posture from the start. It needs a Deployment per role, the migrate Job, PDBs that respect the singletons, `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` above FARM_SHUTDOWN_GRACE, and a DaemonSet-shaped story for the watchdog that is not a DaemonSet, because the hosts are outside the cluster.

**10. Run `internal/node` and `internal/topo` against real hardware.** They compile everywhere and refuse clearly where they cannot work, but neither has met a phone. Cannot be scheduled before 1 and 2.

**11. The mTLS fence proxy.** The largest piece, and the only gap that is currently compensated: the fence is enforced in the database and honoured by the client. Last, because it should be designed against a farm where 1, 2 and 10 have already shipped.

sections.heading: Gaps closed since this page was written
sections.body:
The gap list below was written against an earlier tree, and part of it has since been fixed. Those entries are recorded here rather than deleted: a reader who remembers a gap needs to be able to tell **fixed** from **never there**, and the change that closed one is usually the shortest true description of what the behaviour is now.

The rule for this table is the rule for the gap list itself. An entry moves here only after the code was read and the claim checked against it, never because a commit message said so — which is exactly how the list went stale in the first place. Everything still open is in **What is not built here**, immediately below.

rows: The API was open and could not be closed by configuration. `cmd/farmd/roles.go` appended `api.WithAuthenticator(api.NewAllowAll(log, "anonymous"))` unconditionally, and `api.AuthenticatorFromEnv` — the function that reads `FARM_API_TOKENS` — had no caller, so the remedy `/api/v1/capabilities` printed did nothing.

`cmd/farmd/roles.go:187` now calls `api.AuthenticatorFor(cfg, log)`. It reads `FARM_API_TOKENS` and `FARM_API_AUTH`, builds a `StaticBearer`, and REFUSES to start an exposed listener with no credentials rather than booting open — an api that will not start is recorded as a control-plane gap and refunded onto every live lease, which booting open is not. `internal/api/auth_wiring.go`, with `internal/api/auth_test.go` behind it.

`farmd node` could not start at all, on any platform. `runNode` passed `Addr: cfg.NodeAddr` and never passed `Token`, `node.New` refuses whenever `Addr != "" && Token == ""`, and `FARM_NODE_ADDR` could not be blanked because an empty value reads as unset and returns the `:8082` default — so no environment satisfied the guard.

`cmd/farmd/roles.go:600` passes `FARM_NODE_TOKEN`. The guard itself is right and stays: an unauthenticated endpoint that power-cycles USB ports is worse than no endpoint. Serving nothing is still a legitimate deployment — an empty `Addr` needs no token, and discovery and enrollment run either way.

Recovery tiers 3 (`usb_reset`) and 4 (`port_power`) could never execute. `cmd/farmd/roles.go` constructed `recovery.NewADBActuator(log, nil)` — a nil `HostRunner` — for every role, nothing in the tree spoke `POST /node/v1/usb-reset` or `/node/v1/port-power`, and `farm.hosts` had no column saying where an agent listens.

`internal/node/client.go` is that client, `migrations/00006_node_endpoint.sql` adds `farm.hosts.node_endpoint` and `node_version` so the ladder can find an agent, and `cmd/farmd/roles.go:278-299` wires a real `HostRunner` when one is configured. A farm with no agents still refuses the rungs with a reason rather than reporting them as ineffective.

Dynamic enrollment could not run in any deployable shape: `enroll.New` had exactly one construction site, inside `runNode`, and `runNode` could not start. A handset plugged into a host would never join the fleet, on any deployment.
`runNode` starts now, so the one construction site is reachable. Enrollment is still confined to that role and that role is still Linux-only — see the gaps below for what that costs.

No Helm chart and no Kubernetes manifests. `deploy/helm` was an empty directory and `docker-compose.yml` was the only deployment artifact in the repository, while the README's architecture diagram showed the control plane in Kubernetes.

`deploy/helm/device-farmer` ships a chart for the six control-plane roles plus the migrate Job that has to succeed before any of them start, with a `ServiceMonitor`, secret and configmap templates, and a README that explains why `farmd node` cannot be a workload in it. `values.yaml` documents each knob inline.

`FARM_COMPONENT` is honoured by the `api` role only. `cmd/farmd/roles.go` hardcodes `Component:` for scheduler (214), reaper (230), janitor (255), recovery (300), watchdog (328, `"watchdog:"+hostID`), jobrunner (519), enroll (566) and node (582). Only `runAPI` passes `cfg` through to something that beats `cfg.Component`. The node case is the worst of them: `Component: "node"` discards `internal/node`'s own `"node:" + hostID` default.

Every role resolves its name through `cfg.ComponentFor`, and `roleComponents` records which heartbeat rows each role actually writes — which is what lets the BLOCKER 8 assertion cover a process running six components, and what a name added to `FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS` now buys. `config.TestRoleComponentsCoversEveryRole` fails if a new role is added without saying what it beats as.

`FARM_METRICS_ADDR` binds nothing, no role prints `config.Summary()`, and `FARM_SHUTDOWN_GRACE` is read by one file. `MetricsAddr` appears only in config.go and the summary string; `/metrics` is served on `FARM_API_ADDR`. `Summary()`'s only call site is inside `notImplemented()` (`cmd/farmd/main.go:251`), which has no callers. `cfg.ShutdownGrace` has exactly one consumer, `internal/api/server.go:459`.

Every role binds a `/metrics` listener BEFORE starting its work, so a taken port is a startup failure naming the variable rather than a role that comes up healthy and exports nothing — observed exactly once during verification, when a second process found :9090 held. `cmd/farmd/main.go` also prints `cfg.Summary()` at startup for every role.

Role metrics are defined and never registered. `cmd/farmd/roles.go:86` calls `obs.RegisterAll(reg, log)` with no variadic groups, and the signature is `RegisterAll(r, log, groups ...[]prometheus.Collector)` — so the registry receives internal/obs's own nine collectors and nothing else. Ten packages define `Collectors()` (adbwire, enroll, janitor, jobrunner, node, reaper, recovery, scheduler, topo, watchdog) and the whole tree holds exactly ONE call site: `internal/api/server.go:369`, for adbwire — and that line sits inside `if ownRegistry`, a branch `farmd` never takes, because `runAPI` supplies the registry itself at `roles.go:138`. The process and Go runtime collectors ARE registered — `newRegistry` adds them at `cmd/farmd/roles.go:94-95`, deliberately in the binary rather than in the library, so two roles in one process do not collide over them.
`newRegistry` passes all ten groups to `obs.RegisterAll`, guarded by a test that fails the build when a new package's group is left off.
Exit code 3 (`not implemented`) is documented and unreachable. `notImplemented()` at `cmd/farmd/main.go:238` has no callers, because every committed role is now wired.

Removed, with the reason written down where the codes are: every role dispatches so nothing could return it, and the number is not free — `farmd ctl` exits 3 when the remote REFUSED an action, which is a 409 and therefore an answer rather than a failure. Two meanings for one number in one binary is how a rollout script comes to read a refusal as a missing feature.

gaps.what: `jobrunner` is in `DefaultReaperComponents` now; `janitor` is not, and that is the right call rather than an oversight — the janitor closes orphaned step rows and is not on the renewal path, so refunding its downtime onto a lease would refund an outage in a plane that cannot extend one. What is left is that nothing states the distinction where an operator adding a component to the watch list would read it.
gaps.consequence: If every jobrunner replica is down while api/scheduler/reaper stay healthy, `farm.reaper_arm` records no control-plane gap and refunds nothing. The holders that were renewing those leases are gone with the jobrunners, so at defaults every affected lease is reclaimed 45 minutes later (TTL 15m + grace 30m) and the jobs on the phones are destroyed. This is precisely the BLOCKER 8 mass-reclaim the assertion was written to prevent, reached through a component the assertion does not cover. The janitor is not on the renewal path, so its absence is less costly — but it is equally invisible.

gaps.what: `farm.reaper_arm` is blind to a watched component that has never written a heartbeat row. It computes `SELECT min(h.beat_at) … WHERE h.component = ANY(p_components)` (migrations/00002_lease.sql:439-442); a name with no row contributes nothing to the minimum rather than being treated as infinitely stale.
gaps.consequence: Combined with the previous two gaps this is how the accounting degrades quietly. Under `farmd all` against a fresh database, `cfg.Component` is "all" and nothing ever writes an `api` row, so gap accounting silently covers 2 of the 3 watched names and no error is raised anywhere. There is no alert for "a component I am watching has never beaten" — check `SELECT component FROM farm.component_heartbeat` against FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS by hand after any deployment change.

gaps.what: `all` and `demo` name their API heartbeat after the role. `config.Load("all")` yields component `all`; `Load("demo")` yields `demo`. Neither is on `onRenewalPath`, so both pass preflight, and neither is in the default watch list.
gaps.consequence: Under `farmd all` — the documented single-node shape — the API's heartbeat is written as `all` and is invisible to gap accounting, while scheduler and reaper beat under watched names. An API that wedges while the rest of the process runs produces fresh beats, no recorded gap, and no refund for external holders whose renewals go through HTTP. Set `FARM_COMPONENT=api` and add `all` to `FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS`, or run the roles separately. On `farmd demo` the effect is masked: the demo simulation itself beats api/reaper/scheduler, so the table looks complete when it is not.

gaps.what: Two of the three reach their destination: `FARM_LEASE_RENEW_INTERVAL` is passed through `jobrunner.Config.HolderConfig`, and `FARM_COMPONENT` reaches every role. `FARM_LEASE_WITNESS_INTERVAL` still paces nothing, because no role starts a witness loop — and `config.Summary()` says exactly that at startup (`NOT STARTED`) rather than printing the interval as though it were in force.
gaps.consequence: Tuning the renewal interval to survive a slow Postgres changes nothing, while `config.Summary()` and `/api/v1/capabilities` both report the value you set as if it were in force. The on-device witness — the mechanism that would protect a lease when the control plane is blind — is not running: `witness_at` is NULL on every lease and `witness_extensions` has never exceeded 0. Leases are protected only by TTL+grace and the gap refund.

gaps.what: `docker compose --profile farm up -d` also starts the demo. The `demo` service has no `profiles:` key, and both `demo` and `api` publish `${FARM_PORT:-8420}`.
gaps.consequence: The documented command for a real farm starts simulated hardware writing into the same database as the real control plane, and the second of the two services to start fails to bind 8420. Workaround today: `docker compose --profile farm up -d --scale demo=0`. `docker compose --profile farm config` will show you this before you deploy, without a daemon.

gaps.what: The design and a testable skeleton exist — `docs/design/fence-proxy.md` and `internal/fenceproxy`, 24 tests — and NOTHING CONSTRUCTS EITHER, so no ADB byte in this farm passes through a proxy today. The package is deliberately inert: it imports no database driver, no HTTP client and not the package that owns leases, and two of its tests enforce that (one asserts `FenceSource` has exactly one method, because a second is what would let a refusal DO something; the other parses every file and fails on an identifier naming an act that ends a lease). Integration is the remaining work.
gaps.consequence: A buggy or malicious client that ignores its own fence can still drive a device it no longer owns over ADB, because ADB itself has no notion of the fence. `FARM_NODE_SELF_FENCE_TIMEOUT` and `FARM_SLOT_REARM` exist to bound that window, which is why the rearm assertion is a startup failure rather than a warning. This is the one gap that is currently compensated rather than merely absent.

gaps.what: `internal/node` and `internal/topo` have never run against real hardware. `internal/node/hostops.go` and `internal/node/uhubctl.go` carry `//go:build linux`; `internal/topo/sysfs.go` has no build tag and refuses at runtime instead. All of them compile everywhere, and `internal/node/client_test.go` now exercises the wire protocol against a fake server — which proves the client, not the hardware.
gaps.consequence: Everything the docs say about USB path discovery, USBDEVFS_RESET, uhubctl behaviour and the Linux 6.0 kernel floor is derived from the code and the kernel's documented behaviour, not from a phone. Budget a bring-up period on the first physical host. The binary can start the agent now, so that bring-up is possible — it just has not happened.

gaps.what: The chart has a Deployment for `api`, `scheduler`, `reaper`, `recovery`, `jobrunner` and `watchdog`, and none for `janitor` — which the binary has had since the step model landed, and which is the only thing that closes a `farm.job_steps` row whose process died. A Kubernetes deployment from this chart accumulates orphaned step rows that poison the jobrunner's own claim predicate. It now also ships a `PrometheusRule` beside the `ServiceMonitor`.
gaps.consequence: On a Kubernetes install nothing closes an orphaned row: a jobrunner evicted mid-step leaves its `farm.job_steps` row at `running` and its job at `running` forever, which is the exact condition `internal/janitor` was written to repair, absent from the only deployment artifact that would run it. Add a Deployment for `farmd janitor` — it is a singleton with a leadership lock, like the reaper. And an operator following the README will not expect their tokens to take effect, and will not understand why a token-less api pod refuses to start instead of booting open, which is now the deliberate behaviour.
